{{Short description|Generalization of covers}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''branched covering''' is a map that is almost a [[covering map]], except on a small set.

==In topology==
In topology, a map is a ''branched covering'' if it is a covering map everywhere except for a [[nowhere dense set]] known as the branch set. Examples include the map from a [[Rose (topology)|wedge of circles]] to a single circle, where the map is a [[homeomorphism]] on each circle.

==In algebraic geometry==

In [[algebraic geometry]], the term '''branched covering''' is used to describe [[morphism]]s <math>f</math> from an [[algebraic variety]] <math>V</math> to another one <math>W</math>, the two [[dimension of an algebraic variety|dimension]]s being the same, and the typical fibre of <math>f</math> being of dimension 0.

In that case, there will be an open set <math>W'</math> of <math>W</math> (for the [[Zariski topology]]) that is [[Dense set|dense]] in <math>W</math>, such that the restriction of <math>f</math> to  <math>W'</math> (from <math>V' = f^{-1}(W')</math> to <math>W'</math>, that is) is '''[[Ramification (mathematics)|unramified]]'''.{{clarify|reason=It is unclear whether 0 belongs to ''W&prime;'' in the case of the projection over the ''x'' axis of the hyperbola ''xy'' = 1|date=June 2017}} Depending on the context, we can take this as [[local homeomorphism]] for the [[strong topology]], over the [[complex number]]s, or as an [[étale morphism]] in general (under some slightly stronger hypotheses, on [[flat module|flatness]] and [[Separable extension|separability]]). Generically, then, such a morphism resembles a [[covering space]] in the topological sense. For example, if <math>V</math> and <math>W</math> are both compact [[Riemann surface]]s, we require only that <math>f</math> is holomorphic and not constant, and then there is a finite set of points <math>P</math> of <math>W</math>, outside of which we do find an honest covering

:<math>V' \to W'</math>.

===Ramification locus===
The set of exceptional points on <math>W</math> is called the '''ramification locus''' (i.e. this is the complement of the largest possible open set <math>W'</math>). In general [[monodromy]] occurs according to the [[fundamental group]] of  <math>W'</math> acting on the sheets of the covering (this topological picture can be made precise also in the case of a general base field).

An '''unramified covering''' then is the occurrence of an empty ramification locus.

===Kummer extensions===
Branched coverings are easily constructed as [[Kummer extension]]s, i.e. as [[algebraic extension]] of the [[function field of an algebraic variety|function field]]. The [[hyperelliptic curve]]s are prototypic examples.

==Examples==
===Elliptic curve===
Morphisms of curves provide many examples of ramified coverings. For example, let {{math|''C''}} be the [[elliptic curve]] of equation
:<math>y^2 - x(x-1)(x-2)=0.</math>
The projection of  {{math|''C''}} onto the {{math|''x''}}-axis is a ramified cover with ramification locus given by
:<math>x(x-1)(x-2)=0.</math>
This is because for these three values of {{math|''x''}} the fiber is the double point <math>y^2=0,</math> while for any other value of {{math|''x''}}, the fiber consists of two distinct points (over an [[algebraically closed field]]).

This projection induces an [[algebraic extension]] of degree two of the [[function field of an algebraic variety|function fields]]:
Also, if we take the fraction fields of the underlying commutative rings, we get the morphism
:<math>\mathbb{C}(x) \to \mathbb{C}(x)[y]/(y^2 - x(x-1)(x-2))</math>
Hence this projection is a degree 2 branched covering. This can be homogenized to construct a degree 2 branched covering of the corresponding projective elliptic curve to the projective line.

===Plane algebraic curve===

The previous example may be generalized to any [[algebraic plane curve]] in the following way.
Let {{math|''C''}} be a plane curve defined by the equation {{math|1=''f''(''x'',''y'') = 0}}, where {{math|''f''}}  is a [[separable polynomial|separable]] and [[irreducible polynomial|irreducible]] polynomial in two indeterminates. If {{math|''n''}} is the degree of {{math|''f''}} in {{math|''y''}}, then the fiber consists of {{math|''n''}} distinct points, except for a finite number of values of {{math|''x''}}. Thus, this projection is a branched covering of degree {{math|''n''}}.

The exceptional values of {{math|''x''}} are the roots of the coefficient of <math>y^n</math> in {{math|''f''}}, and the roots of the [[discriminant]] of {{math|''f''}} with respect to {{math|''y''}}.

Over a root {{math|''r''}} of the discriminant, there is at least a ramified point, which is either a [[critical point (mathematics)|critical point]] or a [[singular point of an algebraic variety|singular point]]. If {{math|''r''}} is also a root of the coefficient of <math>y^n</math> in {{math|''f''}}, then this ramified point is "[[point at infinity|at infinity]]".

Over a root {{math|''s''}} of the coefficient of <math>y^n</math> in {{math|''f''}}, the curve {{math|''C''}} has an infinite branch, and the fiber at {{math|''s''}} has less than {{math|''n''}} points. However, if one extends the projection to the [[projective completion]]s of {{math|''C''}} and the {{math|''x''}}-axis, and if {{math|''s''}} is not a root of the discriminant, the projection becomes a covering over a neighbourhood of {{math|''s''}}.

The fact that this projection is a branched covering of degree {{math|''n''}} may also be seen by considering the [[function field of an algebraic variety|function fields]]. In fact, this projection corresponds to the [[field extension]] of degree {{math|''n''}}
:<math>\mathbb C(x) \to \mathbb C(x)[y]/f(x,y).</math>

===Varying Ramifications===
We can also generalize branched coverings of the line with varying ramification degrees. Consider a polynomial of the form
:<math>f(x,y) = g(x)</math>
as we choose different points <math>x=\alpha</math>, the fibers given by the vanishing locus of <math>f(\alpha,y) - g(\alpha)</math> vary. At any point where the multiplicity of one of the linear terms in the factorization of <math>f(\alpha,y) - g(\alpha)</math> increases by one, there is a ramification.

==Scheme Theoretic Examples==
===Elliptic Curves===
Morphisms of curves provide many examples of ramified coverings of schemes. For example, the morphism from an affine elliptic curve to a line
:<math>\text{Spec}\left( {\mathbb{C}[x,y]}/{(y^2 - x(x-1)(x-2)} \right) \to \text{Spec}(\mathbb{C}[x])</math>
is a ramified cover with ramification locus given by
:<math>X = \text{Spec}\left({\mathbb{C}[x]}/{(x(x-1)(x-2))} \right)</math>
This is because at any point of <math>X</math> in <math>\mathbb{A}^1</math> the fiber is the scheme
:<math>\text{Spec}\left({\mathbb{C}[y]}/{(y^2)} \right)</math>
Also, if we take the fraction fields of the underlying commutative rings, we get the [[field homomorphism]]
:<math>\mathbb{C}(x) \to {\mathbb{C}(x)[y]}/{(y^2 - x(x-1)(x-2))},</math>
which is an [[algebraic extension]] of degree two;
hence we got a degree 2 branched covering of an elliptic curve to the affine line. This can be homogenized to construct a morphism of a projective elliptic curve to <math>\mathbb{P}^1</math>.

===Hyperelliptic curve===
A [[hyperelliptic curve]] provides a generalization of the above degree <math>2</math> cover of the affine line,  by considering the affine scheme defined over <math>\mathbb C</math> by a polynomial of the form
:<math>y^2 - \prod(x-a_i)</math> where <math>a_i \neq a_j</math> for <math>i\neq j</math>

===Higher Degree Coverings of the Affine Line===
We can generalize the previous example by taking the morphism
:<math>\text{Spec}\left( \frac{\mathbb{C}[x,y]}{(f(y) - g(x))} \right) \to \text{Spec}(\mathbb{C}[x])</math>
where <math>g(x)</math> has no repeated roots. Then the ramification locus is given by
:<math>X = \text{Spec}\left( \frac{\mathbb{C}[x]}{(f(x))} \right)</math>
where the fibers are given by
:<math>\text{Spec}\left( \frac{\mathbb{C}[y]}{(f(y))} \right)</math>
Then, we get an induced morphism of fraction fields
:<math>\mathbb{C}(x) \to \frac{\mathbb{C}(x)[y]}{(f(y) - g(x))}</math>
There is an <math>\mathbb{C}(x)</math>-module isomorphism of the target with
:<math>\mathbb{C}(x)\oplus\mathbb{C}(x)\cdot y \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathbb{C}(x)\cdot y^{\text{deg}(f(y))} </math>
Hence the cover is of degree <math>\text{deg}(f)</math>.

===Superelliptic Curves===
[[Superelliptic curve]]s are a generalization of hyperelliptic curves and a specialization of the previous family of examples since they are given by affine schemes <math>X/\mathbb{C}</math> from polynomials of the form
:<math>y^k - f(x)</math> where <math>k>2</math> and <math>f(x)</math> has no repeated roots.

===Ramified Coverings of Projective Space===
Another useful class of examples come from ramified coverings of projective space. Given a homogeneous polynomial <math>f \in \mathbb{C}[x_0,\ldots,x_n]</math> we can construct a ramified covering of <math>\mathbb{P}^n</math> with ramification locus
:<math>\text{Proj}\left( \frac{\mathbb{C}[x_0,\ldots,x_n]}{f(x)} \right)</math>
by considering the morphism of projective schemes
:<math>\text{Proj}\left( \frac{\mathbb{C}[x_0,\ldots,x_n][y]}{y^{\text{deg}(f)} - f(x)} \right) \to \mathbb{P}^n</math>
Again, this will be a covering of degree <math>\text{deg}(f)</math>.

==Applications==
Branched coverings <math>C \to X</math> come with a symmetry group of transformations <math>G</math>. Since the symmetry group has stabilizers at the points of the ramification locus, branched coverings can be used to construct examples of orbifolds, or [[Stack (mathematics)|Deligne–Mumford stacks]].
